Abstract Approximately USD 13 trillion are contracted annually by Public Administration, with around 20% of this amount allocated to public works, including infrastructure construction projects. Despite existing regulations, it is not uncommon for public construction projects to experience delays or even abandonment before completion. Such issues not only lead to the waste of public resources but also negatively impact the economic and social development of the affected regions. Although citizens can contribute to Public Works Contract Management (PWCM)—for instance, by monitoring project progress and identifying potential issues—they might lack the necessary understanding of complex concepts required for effective participation. This limitation may result in missed opportunities for timely societal intervention and oversight. This thesis investigates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can support PWCM. Specifically, it explores how AI can model risks, simplify complex project concepts, and communicate them to a non-specialist audience. The study employs a comprehensive approach, encompassing domain understanding, risk prediction, and knowledge dissemination to enhance AI-based support for PWCM. The domain understanding phase involved a Systematic Literature Review (SLR), analyzing 3,252 studies published between 2010 and 2024 to identify primary AI approaches applied in PWCM. This review mapped current AI applications, highlighted gaps related to public contracting phases, application objectives, algorithms used, and features considered in building Machine Learning (ML) models, providing a broad overview of predictive and generative AI techniques in the public works sector. Based on selected findings from the SLR, four ML models were developed and evaluated for predicting contractual failure risks in public works, using data from Paraíba, Brazil. Among these models, Random Forest, employing oversampling for data balancing, showed superior performance, achieving a ROC-AUC value of 0.75. To assist lay users participate in PWCM, an integrated system featuring a chatbot interface was developed to display information about public works and their associated risks. This system utilized a large language model (LLM) to answer user queries in simplified terms, facilitating understanding of project risks and details. Tested with 35 participants of varying PWCM knowledge levels, the chatbot demonstrated notable approval regarding clarity, practical usefulness, accuracy, ease of use, and reliability, thereby improving understanding of PWCM processes. This study advances the knowledge of AI applications in PWCM and provides guidelines for integrating such tools into government systems, thereby promoting more informed citizen participation in public affairs.

title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

Additionally, there are State Courts of Accounts (Tribunais de Contas do Estado; TCE) and municipal courts of accounts, which oversee projects within their respective jurisdictions. These institutions conduct periodic audits, compliance assessments, and can issue sanctions in cases of irregularities. This practice is essential in mitigating risks of deviations and ensuring that projects meaningfully contribute to socioeconomic development, aligning with the strategic objectives of public policies [5]. Efforts to mitigate the effects of potential risks in the contracting process are a focal point for both public administration officials and researchers [6]. The concept of “risk” in our society has multiple definitions. Generally, risk can be understood as the possibility of an event occurring that may lead to negative consequences, uncertainties, or losses, affecting individuals, organizations, or systems in different contexts. In this thesis, a risk can be defined as an event of rescission or annulment of the administrative contract which, if it occurs, will result in the discontinuation of the execution of a project. The modern concept of risk management emerged in the 1950s [7]. Since then, this topic has been gaining prominence in public sector literature [8]. In the field of Public Works Contract Management (PWCM), managing risks encompasses a series of processes, systems, and administrative structures, serving as a mechanism to identify, assess, and support decision-making to mitigate potential threats. PWCM involves various monitoring and control activities carried out using different methods and tools [3]. In loco inspections are a common practice and include on-site visits by inspectors or auditors who verify the project's physical progress, and then compare completed stages with the schedule established in the contract. During these visits, aspects such as the materials' conformity, the execution of services, and compliance with technical specifications are analyzed. In addition to on-site inspections, monitoring is also conducted with the support of digital tools. Efforts to mitigate the effects of potential risks in the contracting process are a focal point for both public administration officials and researchers [6]. The concept of “risk” in our society has multiple definitions. Generally, risk can be understood as the possibility of an event occurring that may lead to negative consequences, uncertainties, or losses, affecting individuals, organizations, or systems in different contexts. In this thesis, a risk can be defined as an event of rescission or annulment of the administrative contract which, if it occurs, will result in the discontinuation of the execution of a project. The modern concept of risk management emerged in the 1950s [7]. Since then, this topic has been gaining prominence in public sector literature [8]. In the field of Public Works Contract Management (PWCM), managing risks encompasses a series of processes, systems, and administrative structures, serving as a mechanism to identify, assess, and support decision-making to mitigate potential threats. PWCM involves various monitoring and control activities carried out using different methods and tools [3]. In loco inspections are a common practice and include on-site visits by inspectors or auditors who verify the project's physical progress, and then compare completed stages with the schedule established in the contract. During these visits, aspects such as the materials' conformity, the execution of services, and compliance with technical specifications are analyzed. In addition to on-site inspections, monitoring is also conducted with the support of digital tools. Internal management and auditing systems enable public managers to access detailed data on each stage of the contracting

3
and execution process, such as records of measurements, payments, and contractual adjustments. These systems centralize project information, facilitating remote monitoring and data cross-referencing to identify potential discrepancies or inconsistencies. In addition to oversight by control agencies, several portals are also available for the public (e.g., citizens and non-profit organizations) to monitor the progress of public works. In Brazil, for example, the National Public Procurement Portal [9] centralizes information on bids and contracts, providing access to raw data and performance indicators. Citizens can utilize platforms such as the Public Works Panel [10] of TCE-PB and the Panel for Monitoring Suspended Works [11] of TCU to monitor the progress and compliance of public works, access details about the companies involved, and follow suspended projects along with their reasons and budgetary impacts. Internationally, platforms like Redflags.eu [12] and Opentender.eu [13] in Europe provide similar monitoring tools with detailed data and risk indicators, promoting transparency and public oversight in many countries. However, despite the availability of these monitoring tools and the stringent rules established in the public contracting process, it is not uncommon to find projects left unfinished due to contract termination or annulment. In 2023 (see Figure 1), in Brazil, the TCU's Panel for Monitoring Suspended Works reported 2,726 unfinished works, representing 18% of the total 15,128 works in progress. These unfinished projects account for an estimated investment of R$ 2.33 billion, out of a total of R$ 83.75 billion allocated for all works nationwide. In the state of Paraíba specifically, 13.4% of the works remain unfinished, resulting in more than R$ 72 million in unutilized funds. Figure 1. Overview of Incomplete Public Works in Brazil.

title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

Additionally, challenges such as corruption and mismanagement remain significant obstacles. In some countries, it is estimated that up to 30% of the funds allocated for public works may be compromised by corrupt practices, amounting to a financial loss of approximately 750 billion dollars [15]. Such instances of corruption undermine the quality and completion of public works and erode public trust in the contracting processes and the management of public resources.
1.2 Problem Definition PWCM faces considerable challenges that go beyond technical and logistical issues [2]. Public procurement involves a growing volume of data and interconnected variables, making the planning, execution, and oversight stages increasingly complex [16, 14, 17, 18]. Although in loco inspections, manual analyses and traditional tools are effective for processing and organizing information, they have limitations when dealing with procurement processes' unpredictability and dynamic nature. Many decisions rely on analyzing multiple factors over time, whose relationships are not always direct or easily identifiable through conventional approaches (e.g., manual review of reports and financial statements, rule-based monitoring systems, and spreadsheet-based tracking tools used for oversight and compliance analysis) [8]. Errors, fraud, inefficiencies, and difficulties in accurately estimating prices often do not follow fixed patterns, making their anticipation and mitigation challenging when using only predefined rules and human review [4, 14, 19]. Furthermore, the number of managed contracts has grown significantly, while the availability of human resources has not always increased at the same rate [20]. This reality requires managers to analyze a large volume of information in a timely manner to ensure process efficiency and compliance. In this scenario, it becomes essential to adopt tools capable of overcoming these limitations, providing greater predictive capacity and a more accessible and comprehensive analysis of public procurement processes [21]. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers a promising approach to improve PWCM by providing enhanced analytical capabilities and more precise decision-making processes

[22, 23, 24]. In particular, Machine Learning (ML), a subfield of AI, expands these capabilities by enabling the processing of large volumes of data and the identification of patterns that may not be evident through traditional methods. These technologies can learn from historical data and continuously improve their predictions as new data is incorporated. Rather than replacing professional analysis, these indicators can serve as support, enabling a more agile and proactive identification of potential risks without compromising the integrity and quality of traditional oversight. This integrated use of predictive modeling technologies represents an opportunity to strengthen the ability to anticipate and mitigate risks in public contracts, aligning with traditional practices while enhancing their effectiveness. Numerous studies have utilized AI to investigate different aspects of public works, specifically focusing on predictive activities using ML [21]. Despite this, even when aiming to make predictions as a primary activity, these studies vary in terms of focus, purpose, and technical challenges. Variations in terms of focus correspond to the granularity of the data used in the studies; that is, while some studies employed models considering the entire area of contracting, others focused on specific areas such as the contracting of construction works [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. In terms of purposes, the objectives of the studies concentrated on specific subjects like the estimation of execution time [30, 31, 28] and costs [25, 26, 31, 32, 29], estimation of the winning bid value [27, 26, 25], and risk of contractual failure [33, 34], among others. Finally, regarding technical challenges, variations exist due to distinctions between algorithms used, features, evaluation metrics, and the level of detail in the development process employed. Recent research [33, 35, 36] suggest that the specificity of predictions is subjective and depends on the contracting context. While these advances have contributed to the field's evolution, some studies have yet to comprehensively explore the evaluation of variables representing different dimensions of contractors' behavior and operations. Factors such as participant profiles, penalty history, bidding characteristics, company attributes, geographical activity, and project features can influence organizational reliability and the likelihood of contractual failures. Research in other public sector contexts indicates that incorporating these elements can enhance predictive models' accuracy and contextual relevance, expanding their applicability for risk analysis and decision-making [37].

Their results can be disseminated through various means, such as government portals, reports, and monitoring organization websites, enabling the interested public to track project progress and associated risks with accuracy. title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.
keywords: Modelos de linguagem de grande escala

Systems that utilize ML are often referred to as 'black boxes' due to the complexity involved in understanding the logic behind their outcomes, creating challenges for building trust and ensuring accountability for the decisions they influence [38] [39]. Their results can be disseminated through various means, such as government portals, reports, and monitoring organization websites, enabling the interested public to track project progress and associated risks with accuracy. Predictive models can be utilized by various stakeholders, including researchers in academia, governmental entities, and regulatory agencies, serving a broad range of users beyond just government institutions [40] [41]. For example, consider a machine learning-based system that displays information on public works and presents the contractual failure risk of each project. Public managers can use the system to monitor project progress and anticipate preventive measures in the face of high risk. Oversight and regulatory bodies, such as courts of accounts offices, can interpret the results to support audits and investigations into potential irregularities. Contracted companies can use the information to adjust risk management strategies and ensure compliance with deadlines and contractual obligations. Citizens and civil society organizations can access the data through transparency portals to track project execution and assess potential impacts on public service delivery. Additionally, researchers and public policy experts can analyze the patterns identified by the system to propose improvements in procurement and project management processes. The effectiveness of predictive models is directly linked to the ability of stakeholders to comprehend the information presented [38]. Additionally, the technical information regarding public works may also demand such expertise, making public engagement even more challenging [42]. Thus, a central component of this effectiveness is structuring processes that integrate strategies aimed at facilitating understanding for different audiences, particularly those with little or no technical knowledge. In this context, the availability of clear and accessible information plays a key role in preventing resource waste, delays, and inefficiencies that impact society [42]. This is because such availability might enable the population to acquire adequate knowledge and contribute to PWCM by acting as ad-hoc inspectors and sources of information for regulatory agencies, thereby enhancing these agencies' oversight capabilities cost-effectively. Existing methods for presenting the results of ML models employ various formats depending on the audience and context of use. In transparency platforms and internal management systems, a common approach is to display analyzed contracts in ordered lists, where predictions are presented in additional columns to facilitate pattern

7
identification (e.g.: [13]). Additionally, charts and comparative tables are used to represent probabilistic distributions, making the results more visually accessible (e.g.: [12] [13]). Reports are also generated, combining summarized statistics and predictions to contextualize data and support decision-making (e.g.: [43]). While these approaches aim to enhance interpretability, previous research in other domains, such as medicine, suggests that simplified visual representations are not always effective for practical decision-making [38] [44] [45] [46] . Different stakeholders have distinct needs and inquiries when interpreting predictions [38]. While some require detailed analyses and technical justifications to support audits and oversight, others need more direct and objective information. This diversity poses challenges to result communication, highlighting the need for approaches that make predictions more understandable and adaptable to different user profiles. Communication strategies based on generative AI (GAI) [47] may be relevant in bridging the gap between technical data and applicable knowledge, fostering greater engagement and informed decision-making [40]. In this context, Large Language Models (LLMs), trained on vast volumes of textual data, have the potential to enhance lay individuals' understanding of various issues related to PWCM [48] [39]. Unlike conventional static reports and dashboards, these models can dynamically generate contextualized explanations, adjusting content and complexity based on the audience’s needs. An extension of these models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), enables them to retrieve and utilize information from external sources [48]. These tools can support various everyday applications [39], including disseminating knowledge about public works, a topic that remains underexplored in the academic literature. From the perspective of government regulatory agencies, this challenge constitutes a significant business problem, as it directly impacts the effectiveness of public contract management and the achievement of institutional objectives. The associated technical problem involves the search for methodologies, models, and tools that support the strategic management of contractual failure risks, as well as effective ways to communicate these risks in an accessible manner, fostering citizen engagement as informed and active stakeholders in the PWCM process. This engagement could, in turn, trigger timely and appropriate interventions by regulatory bodies. There is a recognized need to address this technical problem [22].

1.3 Objectives 1.3.1 General The general objective of this study is to investigate how AI can enhance PWCM processes, focusing on improving risk assessment and facilitating the integration of non-experts into specialized knowledge systems. 1.3.2 Specific To achieve this general objective, the study focuses on the following specific objectives: 1. Extract and review the existing literature through a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify key features (also called independent variables), algorithms, metrics, challenges, and datasets associated with predictive AI algorithms in PWCM. Furthermore, the review should examine the use of Generative AI in public procurement, analyzing its key applications and how these solutions are adapted to different objectives. Finally, it should also identify research gaps and future directions, particularly in relation to knowledge dissemination and risk management. 2. Transform data from governmental sources into a structured dataset suitable for training predictive models, identify attributes that may influence the risk of contractual failure in public works projects, and finally, evaluate the performance of ML models developed to predict these contractual failures. 3. Implement and test strategies for the dissemination of complex PWCM-related information, utilizing LLM and RAG to make this information more accessible to non-experts. 1.4 Methodology and Research Questions This study employs a comprehensive methodological approach to explore how AI can enhance PWCM, particularly in the areas of risk modeling and the integration of non-experts into specialized knowledge systems. The methodology is structured around three stages: (i) domain understanding, (ii) risk prediction, and (iii) knowledge dissemination, each guided by specific research questions. Figure 2 provides a summary of the stages included in the methodology adopted in this thesis.

Source: Created by the Author. (i) Domain Understanding: To establish a foundational understanding of the current applications of AI in PWCM, a SLR was conducted. This review followed the PRISMA 2020 guideline [49], a widely recognized framework for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, ensuring a rigorous and transparent review process. These questions focus on identifying AI applications across different phases of public contracts, their objectives, the methods used to enhance stakeholder understanding, and the key research gaps in the field. (ii) Risk Predic5on Focuses on developing and evaluating machine learning models to predict contractual risks in public works. The features used were derived from the domain understanding phase and assessed for their predictive potential. The results and public works data were utilized in the subsequent phase to support knowledge dissemination.
(iii) Knowledge Dissemina5on Involves the development of a system integrating LLMs with RAG to improve accessibility to public works information and estimated risk assessments.

in public works. Four machine learning algorithms - Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), and Stochastic Gradient Boosting (SGB) - were selected for this purpose. These models were trained and tested using data extracted from Brazilian governmental sources. The features used were initially identified during the domain understanding phase and later evaluated for inclusion in the models based on data availability, theoretical relevance to the problem, and their potential to enhance predictive performance. The models were tested and compared using various performance metrics, such as ROC-AUC, to assess their effectiveness in predicting contractual risks. The following research question guides this component: § RQ5: Is it feasible to develop a specialized machine learning model that can assess and predict risks in public works projects? This question aims to explore the feasibility and effectiveness of the developed models in improving risk management within PWCM. (iii) Knowledge Dissemination: To facilitate knowledge dissemination on PWCM, a system based on LLMs integrated with RAG was developed. The web application presents a list of public works contracts, ordered by estimated risk calculated using the best-performing model from the second stage, allowing users to navigate through projects and select specific contracts. For each selected contract, the system displays detailed project information and associated risk estimates. The chatbot integrated into the system was designed to answer users' questions regarding the monitored contracts, utilizing an LLM model combined with RAG. This mechanism enables responses to be generated based on both the system’s internal data and dynamically retrieved external knowledge bases, providing contextualized and detailed explanations. The system evaluation incorporated both quantitative and qualitative feedback. Performance was evaluated using a Likert scale based on clarity, ease of use, accuracy, understanding, and practical value. Additionally, evaluators’ opinions and comments regarding their experience with the application were collected. The following questions guided this topic: § RQ6: Can LLM models assist non-experts in understanding information about public works? § RQ7: How does integrating external information (e.g., processes, models, public works data) through RAG enhance the accuracy of the information provided?
title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

These questions aim to assess whether the AI-driven approach can make complex information more accessible and accurate for non-experts, thereby enhancing public understanding and participation in PWCM processes. By addressing these research questions within each component, the study aims to contribute to the understanding and improvement of PWCM processes through the application of AI, providing insights into risk assessment methodologies and enhancing communication with both expert and non-expert stakeholders. 1.5 Relevance This thesis makes the following contributions: § This research adopts a methodological approach that encompasses domain understanding, predictive risk modeling, and knowledge dissemination in PWCM. The methodological framework employed not only explores the application of AI in risk prediction but also evaluates strategies for organizing and presenting this information to different audiences. Thus, the study contributes to identifying a potential pathway for the practical implementation of these technologies, considering both the development of predictive models and the accessibility and usability of the generated information. § The domain understanding, through a SLR, enables the mapping of predictive and generative techniques applied in PWCM. This includes identifying the objectives already explored, the phases of the contracting process where AI has been utilized, the variables employed in models, and the metrics used to evaluate algorithms. Regarding generative AI, the review examines its main applications, adaptations to different needs, and unresolved challenges. By consolidating results of research carried out over a decade, the review synthesizes existing knowledge, highlighting advancements and gaps to be addressed, contributing to the development of new studies. § The study introduces a predictive model designed to forecast contractual failures in public works projects. Developed and validated with real data, this model enhances the ability to mitigate potential risks in public contract operations. In practical terms, it can support stakeholders in identifying high-risk contracts early, possibly optimizing resource allocation, and implementing preventive measures to ensure smoother project execution and better use of public funds.

§ The study employs LLM and RAG technologies to make complex information more accessible, enabling various stakeholders to better understand contracts and the risks associated with PWCM. Chapter 2 2. Related Work PWCM has been a topic of interest in academic and professional domains due to the impact it brings to Society in general and to the complexity of managing large-scale infrastructure projects [14]. Traditional support approaches often rely on manual methods and specific tools for contract monitoring, risk forecasting, and ensuring compliance with regulations [52]. While effective in specific contexts, these approaches often face challenges in scaling and providing efficiency in dynamic and complex projects [53]. Over time, research has progressed toward integrating data-driven methodologies to enhance decision-making in PWCM [52] [54]. AI has emerged as a transformative tool in public governance, offering solutions for process automation, data management, and predictive modeling [40]. Despite its potential, existing literature often overlooks key aspects necessary for tailoring AI applications to the unique challenges of public works, including the prediction of contractual failures and the effective communication of complex insights to diverse stakeholders. Previous reviews on AI in public governance have primarily examined broad applications, such as process automation and data management in the public sector [55] [56] [57]. Although these reviews offer valuable insights, they lack a unified focus on the methodological and practical aspects critical for developing predictive models, such as selecting and evaluating predictive features, validating models, and addressing contextual factors unique to public works. Additionally, while some efforts, like [40], have explored methods to translate complex predictive insights into accessible formats for non-specialist audiences, detailed examinations of the methodologies and algorithms underlying these approaches remain scarce. Building on the broader gaps identified in previous reviews regarding the integration of AI into the public sector, the specific application of predictive models to address contractual failures in public works represents a particularly underexplored area. Previous studies have employed ML for tasks such as cost prediction [32] [25] [26] [58] [29], fraud detection in bidding processes [24] [16] [35] [23], time estimation extensions [31] [30] [28] [59], and risk of contractual failure [34] [33] [23]. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

Chapter 2 2. Related Work PWCM has been a topic of interest in academic and professional domains due to the impact it brings to Society in general and to the complexity of managing large-scale infrastructure projects [14]. Traditional support approaches often rely on manual methods and specific tools for contract monitoring, risk forecasting, and ensuring compliance with regulations [52]. While effective in specific contexts, these approaches often face challenges in scaling and providing efficiency in dynamic and complex projects [53]. Over time, research has progressed toward integrating data-driven methodologies to enhance decision-making in PWCM [52] [54]. AI has emerged as a transformative tool in public governance, offering solutions for process automation, data management, and predictive modeling [40]. Despite its potential, existing literature often overlooks key aspects necessary for tailoring AI applications to the unique challenges of public works, including the prediction of contractual failures and the effective communication of complex insights to diverse stakeholders. Previous reviews on AI in public governance have primarily examined broad applications, such as process automation and data management in the public sector [55] [56] [57]. Although these reviews offer valuable insights, they lack a unified focus on the methodological and practical aspects critical for developing predictive models, such as selecting and evaluating predictive features, validating models, and addressing contextual factors unique to public works. Additionally, while some efforts, like [40], have explored methods to translate complex predictive insights into accessible formats for non-specialist audiences, detailed examinations of the methodologies and algorithms underlying these approaches remain scarce. Building on the broader gaps identified in previous reviews regarding the integration of AI into the public sector, the specific application of predictive models to address contractual failures in public works represents a particularly underexplored area. Previous studies have employed ML for tasks such as cost prediction [32] [25] [26] [58] [29], fraud detection in bidding processes [24] [16] [35] [23], time estimation extensions [31] [30] [28] [59], and risk of contractual failure [34] [33] [23]. Despite predictive

efforts and as already mentioned in the Introduction, many studies do not evaluate the relevance of features that capture different dimensions of contractors' behavior and operations, which are pertinent for predicting contractual failures in public works. These dimensions include participation profiles [60], penalty history [34], bidding properties [24], company characteristics [30] [35] , geographical activities [23] [4], and work attributes [32] [25]. Previous studies demonstrate that multidimensional factors are associated with risk and organizational reliability in other public sector contexts [37], justifying their inclusion for more accurate and contextually adapted (e.g., PWCM) models. Evaluating these features in the context of public works can enhance the understanding of factors impacting contractual performance, supporting the adaptation of predictive models to the sector's practical needs, and identifying relevant patterns to aid decision-making. The application of AI in public works management represents a significant advancement in addressing challenges. However, while relevant to the context, these approaches often lack the ability to effectively communicate complex insights to non-specialist stakeholders. More recently, generative models, particularly LLMs, have been widely applied in various legal and contractual information management contexts. Previous studies have explored the use of LLMs to manage legal datasets in public procurement processes [61], facilitate the evaluation of bids in tenders [62], analyze and summarize legal contracts [63], detect risks and assess complex construction contracts [64] [65], as well as extract adjudication criteria in Swiss tenders [66]. These applications highlight the potential of LLMs to process and simplify intricate information in government documents. However, existing research has predominantly focused on technical applications aimed at specialists without sufficiently exploring the potential of these models to facilitate the understanding of estimates and risks by both public works managers and citizens with limited knowledge of the subject. The use of these models could not only improve information accessibility for professionals in the field but also enhance public participation, promoting greater transparency and engagement in governance processes and decision-making related to public works. In the context of citizen engagement, there is growing interest in utilizing tools to bridge the gap between technical knowledge and public understanding [67]. Through LLMs, by transforming complex concepts into more accessible language, these models can potentially empower citizens to engage more effectively in decision-making

16
processes. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of LLM-based systems, particularly in chat formats, for simplifying technical documents and providing interactive explanations [64] [65] [68]. These efforts align with the trend toward strengthening participatory governance, although the application of LLMs in the context of PWCM remains limited. The integration of RAG techniques has further expanded the potential of LLMs by addressing one of their main limitations: the tendency to generate imprecise or irrelevant information. RAG combines the generative capabilities of LLMs with external knowledge retrieval systems, improving responses' contextual relevance and accuracy [61]. This technique has proven effective in applications such as legal assistance [61], making it a valuable addition to interactive systems. Despite its advantages, limited literature explores the use of RAG in the context of public works contracts, particularly in solutions designed to foster citizen engagement. LLMs have also been widely adopted in various other domains, including healthcare, education, and finance, where they simplify complex workflows and improve access to specialized knowledge. For instance, LLMs have been employed in healthcare to generate summaries of medical records and assist in patient diagnosis [69]. In education, these models are used for personalized tutoring, simplifying complex subjects for students [39]. In finance, they facilitate contract analysis and generate insights from financial reports [70]. These applications across different fields highlight the adaptability of LLMs in addressing knowledge gaps and enhancing interactivity, offering a parallel to their potential in public works management. The reviewed literature indicates that significant gaps remain in the application of AI in public works management, both from a predictive perspective and in terms of knowledge dissemination. While several studies have demonstrated the potential of ML for predicting contractual risks and of LLMs for interpreting administrative documents, few initiatives comprehensively integrate both approaches. This study aims to advance in this direction by proposing predictive models for identifying risks in public works contracts while exploring how generative AI tools can make this information more accessible to managers and citizens. This approach contributes to the literature by integrating quantitative and qualitative methods, reinforcing the role of AI in enhancing transparency and efficiency in public administration. Table 1 presents a comparison between previous research and the contributions of this study on AI applications in PWCM, highlighting gaps in the literature and advancements proposed.

Theoretical Foundation 3.1 Problem and Proposed Solution Formalization To formalize the problem that this research aims to investigate, it is essential to address the issues along each of the three technical solution components within the PWCM process: domain understanding, risk prediction, and knowledge dissemination. To achieve domain understanding, a SLR was conducted. A SLR aims to retrieve a subset 𝐿⊆𝐷, where 𝐷 is the total set of documents in the domain. The subset 𝐿 is obtained based on well-defined criteria, with inclusion criteria denoted by 𝐶! and exclusion criteria by 𝐶#, ensuring that only relevant documents are included. From each selected work, the proposed targets and features are extracted for analysis. The targets are collectively defined as 𝑇={𝑡$,𝑡%,…,𝑡&} and represent the key outcomes, such as risk prediction, cost estimation, and execution time estimation. Here, these targets guide the development of predictive models within the context of public works contracts. In addition to the targets, the features represent the input variables for the models. They are defined as 𝐹∗={𝑓∗$,𝑓∗%,…,𝑓∗!}, encompassing the various factors that influence the outcomes. A dataset from Brazilian government databases, denoted as 𝑃, consists of items or records {𝑝$,𝑝%,…,𝑝(}, with each item representing a public works contract and its associated data. A subset 𝐹⊆𝐹∗ was chosen, focusing on features relevant for evaluation of the contractual risk estimator. This subset 𝐹 serves as the basis for constructing the input space R), where 𝑑 is the number of features in 𝐹. In other words, the subset 𝐹 defines the dimensions of R), forming the input vectors used by the ML models. The aim of this selection was to identify key variables that could improve prediction accuracy, including some not previously explored in the literature. Based on these features, four different ML models - ANN, LR, RF, and SGB - were developed to predict the risk of public works contractual failure. Each model was selected for its demonstrated effectiveness in similar contexts: ANN for modeling complex nonlinear relationships, RF for its robustness against overfitting, LR for its straightforward interpretability, and SGB for its capability to progressively minimize prediction errors. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

and language [72]. The field of AI emerged from the effort to replicate these abilities in machines, using computational approaches to develop systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally require human cognition [73]. In 1950, Alan Turing published the article Computing Machinery and Intelligence [74], discussing whether machines could exhibit intelligent behavior. He proposed the Turing Test, a conceptual experiment designed to evaluate whether a machine could imitate human communication well enough to be indistinguishable from a human in a text-based dialogue. This work established a theoretical foundation for studies on machine-human interaction, influencing research in ML and NLP. The recognition of AI as a scientific discipline took place at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956, organized by John McCarthy [75]. This event brought together researchers aiming to build systems capable of imitating human intelligence. Following this meeting, the first laboratories dedicated to AI research emerged, and the term “artificial intelligence” was formally adopted [76]. The enthusiasm surrounding AI led to significant early advancements, highlighting the potential for machines to emulate intelligent human behaviors. In 1952, Arthur Samuel developed a checkers-playing computer program capable of learning and improving its performance to a degree that challenged amateur human players, demonstrating the viability of machine learning concepts [77]. Shortly thereafter, Newell, Simon, and Shaw created the Logic Theorist, a pioneering program that successfully proved numerous theorems from the Principia Mathematica, introducing fundamental ideas such as heuristic search methods, list processing, and reasoning modeled as search processes [78]. Additionally, in 1957, Frank Rosenblatt developed the Perceptron, a model marking the beginnings of connectionism, laying essential groundwork for the subsequent emergence of neural networks and, eventually, deep learning approaches [79]. Despite early advancements, many AI systems struggled to handle complex problems, leading to the first AI winter - a period of disillusionment and reduced research funding as expectations were not met in practice [76]. However, the 1970s saw the emergence of expert systems, which relied on knowledge bases to make decisions in specific domains [80]. One of the first examples was DENDRAL, developed at Stanford University for automated chemical analysis. 3.2.2 Fundamental Concepts AI is divided into subfields to facilitate specialization and progress in each specific area. Among these are ML, DL, NLP, GAI, and LLMs. Each of these fields has distinct methods for handling different types of data and problems, allowing research and applications to be developed in a more targeted manner. Some of these subfields overlap, enabling the combination of techniques to enhance the efficiency of models in various applications. Figure 3 presents a summary of each specific area, highlighting their relationships and intersections within the field of AI. Figure 3. Hierarchical Structure and Relationships Among AI Subfields.
Source: Created by the Author. ML is a subfield of AI that encompasses several other specific areas. While traditional ML performs on tasks with straightforward relationships, such as cost estimations [54]; DL, a subfield of ML, uses deep neural networks with multiple layers to recognize intricate patterns [83]. For example, DL enables advanced applications like medical image analysis for disease detection [87], where the relationships between inputs and outputs are complex. GAI, a subfield of DL, encompasses models that generate new content, such as text [88], images [89], or music [90]. Deep neural network-based models, such as GANs (e.g., StyleGAN for face generation [91]) and Transformers [84] (e.g., the GPT series for text generation [88]), represent DL-based GAI. It is also important to note that not all GAI is related to NLP, as some models operate in distinct domains, such as DALL-E for generating images [89], and MusicLM for musical composition [90]. NLP focuses on the analysis, understanding, and generation of human language [92], utilizing both DL and simpler statistical methods.

Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

3.2.2 Fundamental Concepts AI is divided into subfields to facilitate specialization and progress in each specific area. Among these are ML, DL, NLP, GAI, and LLMs. Each of these fields has distinct methods for handling different types of data and problems, allowing research and applications to be developed in a more targeted manner. Some of these subfields overlap, enabling the combination of techniques to enhance the efficiency of models in various applications. Figure 3 presents a summary of each specific area, highlighting their relationships and intersections within the field of AI. Figure 3. Hierarchical Structure and Relationships Among AI Subfields.
Source: Created by the Author. ML is a subfield of AI that encompasses several other specific areas. While traditional ML performs on tasks with straightforward relationships, such as cost estimations [54]; DL, a subfield of ML, uses deep neural networks with multiple layers to recognize intricate patterns [83]. For example, DL enables advanced applications like medical image analysis for disease detection [87], where the relationships between inputs and outputs are complex. GAI, a subfield of DL, encompasses models that generate new content, such as text [88], images [89], or music [90]. Deep neural network-based models, such as GANs (e.g., StyleGAN for face generation [91]) and Transformers [84] (e.g., the GPT series for text generation [88]), represent DL-based GAI. It is also important to note that not all GAI is related to NLP, as some models operate in distinct domains, such as DALL-E for generating images [89], and MusicLM for musical composition [90]. NLP focuses on the analysis, understanding, and generation of human language [92], utilizing both DL and simpler statistical methods.

Its focus can be defined as the development of algorithms capable of learning patterns from data without being explicitly programmed for each task [93]. Unlike traditional approaches based on explicit rules, which require the manual definition of criteria and conditions for each situation, ML models automatically adjust their weights (parameters that determine the influence of each input or independent variable on the output prediction) by analyzing patterns in the data from a training set. This learning occurs without directly programming all decision rules, allowing the model to generalize patterns from observed examples and evaluate its performance on a validation or test set. In the context of risk prediction in PCWM, ML models receive a set of attributes representing information related to contractual processes and return an estimate of the risk of failure. The objective of the models is to minimize the prediction error by reducing the difference between observed and predicted values. The goal is to learn a function that relates the input attributes to the target variable, allowing the model to predict new data. This paradigm is subdivided into classification and regression. 24
learning process involves optimizing the model parameters to minimize the difference between predictions and actual values. § Unsupervised learning: Unlike supervised learning, it does not rely on labeled data and aims to identify patterns without needing predefined outputs [93]. This approach can be used for exploratory data analysis and the identification of underlying structures that are not explicitly defined. Clustering methods, for example, allow the grouping of contracts with similar characteristics, enabling the detection of recurring patterns and assisting in the categorization of different types of contracts [17]. § Reinforcement learning: fundamentally differs from the two previous paradigms, as it is based on an agent that learns by interacting with the environment and adjusting its actions according to received rewards [93]. The objective is to improve performance over time by selecting the best actions based on previous outcomes. The ML models used in this study are based on supervised learning and applied to predicting contractual failure risk in public works. Four algorithms were adopted: ANN, LR, RF, and SGB. The subsection below details the motivations for choosing these algorithms and their main characteristics. 3.2.4 Algorithms Used in This Study The ANN, LR, RF, and SGB algorithms were selected for their relevance in other risk prediction problems [4] [24] [34] [19] [35] [59] [94] [22] and their suitability for the characteristics of the data used in this study. LR was chosen for its interpretability and statistical foundation [95] [96], being widely used for probabilistic modeling in binary problems such as contractual failure prediction. ANN was included due to its ability to capture complex nonlinear relationships [97], which is relevant in a context where multiple factors interact to influence risk. Tree-based methods, RF and SGB, were selected for their robustness against overfitting, ability to handle heterogeneous variables, and strong performance on imbalanced datasets [95] [98], such as the one used in this study, where the number of successful contracts significantly exceeds those with failures. The following subsections detail each of the adopted algorithms, highlighting their characteristics.

3.2.4.1 Artificial Neural Networks ANNs can be defined as computational models whose design is rooted in the functioning of biological neural networks in the human brain [94]. The foundational milestone dates to the 1940s with the McCulloch and Pitts model, which introduced a simplified logical representation of the biological neuron, capable of performing Boolean operations [97]. In the 1950s, Frank Rosenblatt developed the Perceptron, a pioneering supervised learning model that adjusted weights based on the errors between predictions and actual values, thereby establishing the foundations for adaptive training [99]. These contributions laid the groundwork for the development of more complex architectures, including modern deep networks that integrate multiple hidden layers. From a biological perspective, neurons are specialized cells for the reception, processing, and transmission of information [100]. Each neuron is composed of different parts, such as the cell body, dendrites, and axon (see Figure 4.a). Dendrites act as signal receptors, while the cell body integrates these signals, determining whether the action potential will be generated. When the signal reaches a certain threshold, the nerve impulse propagates along the axon to the synapses, where neurotransmitters are released to transmit the information to other neurons. This entire process, together with the interconnection between neurons, enables the brain to process information [100]. The ANNs, are simplistically based on the functioning of biological neurons. Artificial neurons are organized into layers: input layer, hidden layer, and output layer. In the input layer of an ANN, each artificial neuron receives the inputs, represented by a vector 𝑥=[𝑥$,𝑥%,…,𝑥-], where each 𝑥! it is a numerical value corresponding to a specific characteristic of the dataset, often referred to as an independent variable. Just as dendrites in a biological neuron capture inputs signals, the artificial neurons in the input layer receive the values 𝑥!, which are weighted by 𝑤! ∈ [0,1] - the strength or relevance of each input in the processing and ∑𝑤!=1-!.$. These data are transmitted to the hidden layers, which process the information. In the hidden layer, each neuron processes the received information through the weighted sum of the inputs. The weights 𝑤! are initially set either randomly or with pre-defined values and are adjusted during training using algorithms such as gradient descent, which minimizes a cost function by iteratively updating the weights based on the computed error. This adjustment refines the weights throughout the supervised learning process, reflecting the relative importance of each input in generating the neuron’s output.

The Gini index measures the impurity of the node, where the lower its value, the greater the homogeneity of the data. The construction of the tree occurs iteratively. Initially, the complete set of contracts is analyzed, and the first split occurs based on the variable that minimizes the impurity of the resulting groups. For example, suppose the variable on previous sanctions is chosen as the first separation criterion because it presents the lowest Gini index. The root node then splits into two branches: contracts with previous sanctions and contracts without sanctions. For each of these subsets, the process is repeated, examining other variables such as the number of amendments, the total number of bids won, and the total value. The division process continues until a stopping criterion is met, such as a minimum number of contracts per node or the minimum impurity. The final nodes of the tree correspond to the leaves, containing the final classification of the contract. Despite its interpretability, a single decision tree can be sensitive to variations in the training data, resulting in models with high variance and susceptible to overfitting [102]. To mitigate this limitation, the RF algorithm combines multiple decision trees, trained using different subsets of data and randomly selected variables. Each tree in the model receives a random sample from the training set (bootstrap sampling), and at each node, a random subset of predictor variables is chosen to determine the split. This approach reduces the correlation between individual trees, increasing the stability and accuracy of the model [103]. Let a set of 𝑃 contracts be represented by a feature vector 𝐹= {𝐹$,𝐹%,…,𝐹,} , where 𝑀 is the total number of available variables. For each tree 𝑇& in the model, a subset 𝐹& ⊂ F is randomly selected for each node split, ensuring diversity in the generated forest of trees. Different values for the number of predictors per node 𝑚 can be tested (𝑚 = 2,5,10,…,𝑛), allowing the exploration of different data structures and the evaluation of their impact on model performance. The final prediction of RF is obtained through majority voting in the case of classification or by averaging the individual predictions in the case of regression [95]. Figure 5 highlights the functioning of the classifier, illustrating the sampling process, the random selection of variables in each tree, and the final decision through majority voting.

title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.
