This model is also less sensitive to imbalanced data compared to more complex models, provided that proper adjustment is applied, such as class weighting [104]. 3.2.4.4 Stochastic Gradient Boosting Gradient Boosting is an ML method based on the principle of sequential and additive learning. It belongs to the family of boosting methods, which combine multiple weak models to form a strong model [98]. In the case of Gradient Boosting, the combination is achieved through the progressive minimization of the error made by previous models. Initially, a base model, usually a decision tree, is trained to make predictions on the dataset. Then, the residuals (differences between the model's predictions and the actual values) are calculated. A new model is trained to predict these residuals, adjusting to reduce the errors of the previous model. This process is repeated iteratively, with each new step reducing the discrepancy between the model's predictions and the actual values. The final model is obtained by summing the predictions of all trained trees, weighted according to their contribution to error minimization. Stochastic Gradient Boosting (SGB) is a variation of this method, proposed by Friedman [105], which introduces a random sampling mechanism during training to reduce the risk of overfitting and improve generalization ability. Unlike traditional Gradient Boosting, where all observations in the training set are used to train each new model in the sequence, SGB randomly selects a fraction of the data in each iteration. Depending on the implementation, this sampling can occur at the instance level (rows of the database) and at the predictor variable level (columns). As a result, each model trained in the sequence learns from a different subset of the data, making training more robust and less prone to excessively fitting specific patterns in the training set.

32
To obtain a model that is better adjusted to the characteristics of the data, some hyperparameters need to be defined during training. The number of trees directly influences the model’s ability to learn patterns in the data. A smaller number may result in a model with a lower capacity to capture complex patterns, while a larger number may lead to a more precise fit but with the risk of overfitting. The depth of the trees, in turn, affects the complexity of the rules the model can learn. Shallower trees capture simpler relationships between predictor variables and the target variable, while deeper trees allow for more detailed representations, potentially increasing the model’s predictive capacity in scenarios where there are more complex interactions in the data. Although SGB shares similarities with other tree-based algorithms, such as RF, there are fundamental differences between the two methods. Both use decision trees and incorporate elements of randomness to improve generalization, but the way they combine individual models is distinct. RF adopts a parallel learning approach, where multiple decision trees are trained independently, each with a random subset of the data and predictor variables. The final prediction is obtained through an aggregation process, usually majority voting for classification. In contrast, SGB follows a sequential scheme, where each tree is trained to correct the errors of the previous one, allowing for a more targeted optimization of predictive error. Based on its characteristics, SGB may be suitable for problems that require predictive models capable of handling complex patterns in the data. The introduction of random sampling during training helps reduce the impact of specific patterns in the dataset, making the model less susceptible to overfitting. Additionally, the method allows for controlling the complexity of the generated trees, which helps mitigate issues caused by outliers that could influence the model’s structure. The partial selection of data in each iteration also favors learning in scenarios where there is an imbalance between classes, reducing bias toward the majority class and improving the model's ability to identify relevant patterns across all categories. 3.2.5 Evaluation of Model Performance ML models aim to make predictions based on historical data. In addition to needing to be accurate, these models must be generalists, meaning they must be capable of generalizing their predictions well to new data. Otherwise, if a model is specific to a dataset, it will struggle to make predictions for different datasets.

There are some techniques for performing this dataset split. The Hold-Out and Cross-Validation techniques are described below The Hold-Out technique divides the dataset into two subsets: one for training the model and another for evaluating (testing) its performance. The most common approach is to use 80% of the data for training the model and the remaining 20% for testing. However, this proportion may vary depending on the availability and size of the dataset, as well as the complexity of the problem under study. Unlike other validation techniques, the data split in the Hold-Out method occurs only once, without resampling, making it a relatively fast and computationally efficient method for training machine learning models. Compared to approaches such as Cross-Validation, Hold-Out requires less computational time, which can be advantageous in scenarios involving large datasets or when model training is particularly costly in terms of processing power [106]. However, this simplicity also represents a significant limitation. A single data split may result in subsets that are not representative of the original distribution, compromising the model’s ability to generalize correctly to new data. If the separation of the subsets is not well-balanced, the model may become biased or exhibit inconsistent performance across different runs. Thus, although the Hold-Out method is widely used due to its speed and ease of implementation, it may not be the best choice when the available dataset is small or when there is high variability in the data. To evaluate the model's performance, it must be tested on an unknown dataset. For this purpose, the dataset is divided into two subsets: one for training and another for testing. The training set is used to train an algorithm, while the test set is used to evaluate the model after learning, ensuring that the model generalizes well to new data. There are some techniques for performing this dataset split. The Hold-Out and Cross-Validation techniques are described below The Hold-Out technique divides the dataset into two subsets: one for training the model and another for evaluating (testing) its performance. The most common approach is to use 80% of the data for training the model and the remaining 20% for testing. However, this proportion may vary depending on the availability and size of the dataset, as well as the complexity of the problem under study. Unlike other validation techniques, the data split in the Hold-Out method occurs only once, without resampling, making it a relatively fast and computationally efficient method for training machine learning models. Compared to approaches such as Cross-Validation, Hold-Out requires less computational time, which can be advantageous in scenarios involving large datasets or when model training is particularly costly in terms of processing power [106]. However, this simplicity also represents a significant limitation. A single data split may result in subsets that are not representative of the original distribution, compromising the model’s ability to generalize correctly to new data. If the separation of the subsets is not well-balanced, the model may become biased or exhibit inconsistent performance across different runs. Thus, although the Hold-Out method is widely used due to its speed and ease of implementation, it may not be the best choice when the available dataset is small or when there is high variability in the data. In such cases, techniques such as Cross-Validation may be more suitable for ensuring more reliable evaluations of model performance [106]. The Cross-Validation process consists of organizing the training data into 𝑘 folds, denoted as 𝐹={ 𝐹$,𝐹%,𝐹5,… ,𝐹& }. Each iteration 𝑖 selects one fold 𝐹! as the validation set, while the remaining 𝑘−1 folds form the training set. Since the data is approximately evenly split, each fold contains about $& of the total training set 𝐷789!-, and the training set in each iteration consists of the remaining 𝑘−1 folds, totaling approximately &1$& of the available data. In each iteration, the model is trained using the 𝑘−1 training folds and then evaluated on the fold reserved for validation. The performance 𝑃! obtained in this step is recorded using relevant metrics, such as accuracy or mean squared error. This

process is repeated 𝑘 times, ensuring that each fold is used exactly once for validation. At the end of the 𝑘 iterations, the final performance of the model is computed as the average of the individual performances from each iteration: 𝑃:!-9;=$& ∑𝑃!&!.$. This approach reduces the influence of unrepresentative data splits and provides a more reliable estimate of the model’s generalization ability. Higher precision values indicate that the model's most positive predictions are correct, reducing the number of incorrect high-risk classifications. However, a model with high precision is not necessarily efficient if it produces a significant number of false negatives, which necessitates the complementary analysis of other metrics [107]. The selection of precision as an evaluation metric is particularly relevant in scenarios where incorrect high-risk classifications lead to high costs. In the context of risk assessment in public works contracts, many incorrect high-risk classifications may result in the misallocation of resources for unnecessary audits or the imposition of restrictive measures on contracts that do not present a significant risk. 3.2.6.2 Recall The recall metric measures the proportion of correctly classified positive instances relative to the total number of instances that belong to the positive class. While precision evaluates the reliability of the model's positive predictions, recall quantifies the model's ability to correctly identify all positive instances, regardless of the number of incorrect predictions for the positive class [107]. In the context of this study, sensitivity answers the following question: Among all contracts that are truly high risk, what percentage is correctly identified by the model? Formally, sensitivity can be defined as: 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 =𝑇𝑃𝑇𝑃+𝐹𝑁 (3) This metric is particularly relevant in scenarios where failing to detect a positive case can have significant consequences. In the context of risk assessment in public works contracts, a model with low sensitivity may fail to identify truly problematic contracts, erroneously classifying them as low risk. 3.2.6.3 Accuracy Accuracy is a metric that measures the model's overall performance, representing the proportion of correct predictions relative to the total number of predictions made. This metric considers both correctly classified positive and negative instances, providing a global assessment of the model’s effectiveness [107]. In the context of this study, accuracy answers the following question: What proportion of high-risk and low-risk contracts were correctly classified?

Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

Higher precision values indicate that the model's most positive predictions are correct, reducing the number of incorrect high-risk classifications. However, a model with high precision is not necessarily efficient if it produces a significant number of false negatives, which necessitates the complementary analysis of other metrics [107]. The selection of precision as an evaluation metric is particularly relevant in scenarios where incorrect high-risk classifications lead to high costs. In the context of risk assessment in public works contracts, many incorrect high-risk classifications may result in the misallocation of resources for unnecessary audits or the imposition of restrictive measures on contracts that do not present a significant risk. 3.2.6.2 Recall The recall metric measures the proportion of correctly classified positive instances relative to the total number of instances that belong to the positive class. While precision evaluates the reliability of the model's positive predictions, recall quantifies the model's ability to correctly identify all positive instances, regardless of the number of incorrect predictions for the positive class [107]. In the context of this study, sensitivity answers the following question: Among all contracts that are truly high risk, what percentage is correctly identified by the model? Formally, sensitivity can be defined as: 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 =𝑇𝑃𝑇𝑃+𝐹𝑁 (3) This metric is particularly relevant in scenarios where failing to detect a positive case can have significant consequences. In the context of risk assessment in public works contracts, a model with low sensitivity may fail to identify truly problematic contracts, erroneously classifying them as low risk. 3.2.6.3 Accuracy Accuracy is a metric that measures the model's overall performance, representing the proportion of correct predictions relative to the total number of predictions made. This metric considers both correctly classified positive and negative instances, providing a global assessment of the model’s effectiveness [107]. In the context of this study, accuracy answers the following question: What proportion of high-risk and low-risk contracts were correctly classified?

Mathematically, accuracy is defined as:
𝑎𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦 =𝑇𝑃+𝑇𝑁𝑇𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 + 𝐹𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁 (4) Although widely used, accuracy may not be the most appropriate metric for evaluating models trained on imbalanced datasets, where one class significantly outnumbers the other. In such cases, a model may achieve high accuracy simply by favoring the majority class without necessarily being effective in identifying instances from the minority class. Therefore, model evaluation should incorporate complementary metrics to ensure a more precise performance assessment. 3.2.6.4 F1-Score The F1-Score is a metric that balances both false positives and false negatives by combining precision (Equation 2) and recall (Equation 3) into a single value. It is calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, ensuring that both metrics are considered simultaneously [107]. Mathematically, the F1-Score is defined as:
𝐹1−𝑆𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒 =2 ⋅ 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 ⋅ 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 + 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 (5) Unlike accuracy, which considers all predictions equally, the F1-Score provides a more balanced assessment in cases where there is an uneven distribution between classes. This metric is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets, as it helps evaluate the model’s performance in identifying the minority class without overemphasizing the majority class. 3.2.6.5 ROC-AUC The Receiver Operating Characteristic - Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) metric is used to evaluate the performance of binary classification models by measuring their ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes correctly [109]. To achieve this, the ROC curve is employed, representing the relationship between recall (Equation 3) and specificity (Equation 6) across different decision thresholds. The area under this curve (AUC) summarizes this information into a single numerical value.

In the context of this research, ROC-AUC was used as the standard metric as it provides a broader perspective on the model’s ability to predict high-risk contracts across different thresholds. 3.2.7 Class Balancing Class balancing is an approach to address imbalanced datasets with a significant disparity in the number of examples between classes. This imbalanced scenario is common in problems related to contract failures, where the number of failed contracts is considerably lower compared to those that were successfully completed. Imbalance can negatively impact the performance of ML algorithms, as models tend to learn patterns predominantly based on the majority class, leading to inaccurate predictions for the minority class. In extreme cases, the model may completely disregard the underrepresented class, making it ineffective in identifying high-risk contracts. To mitigate this issue, different class balancing techniques can be applied during data preprocessing. The most commonly used approaches include undersampling and oversampling. In undersampling, random samples from the majority class are removed until the class proportions become more balanced. In oversampling, random copies of observations from the minority class are generated to increase its representation in the training set. These approaches aim to prevent the model from becoming biased toward the majority class, thereby improving its generalization ability. 3.2.8 Natural Language Processing NLP is a subfield of AI that studies methods and techniques to enable computational systems to understand, process, and generate human language [92]. Models based on NLP are widely used in various applications, such as identifying and correcting grammatical errors, disambiguating word meanings, and extracting information [111]. With the advancement of neural network architectures, LLMs have become central to this field, allowing systems to improve in both language understanding and generation [73]. The evolution of LLMs models has introduced challenges related to the limited knowledge embedded within the models and the generation of inaccurate responses [112]. To address these issues, techniques like RAG have been developed, integrating external information retrieval with text generation to enhance response accuracy [48]. This approach enables models to utilize additional information not present in their pre-trained weights, reducing dependence on internally stored data and aligning responses more closely with external sources. The following sections detail the concepts of LLMs, discuss their architecture and functionality, and explain RAG's integration with generative models to improve the quality of generated responses. 3.2.8.1 Large Language Models LLMs can be defined as DL models trained to process and generate natural language based on large volumes of textual data [47] [69]. These models utilize Transformer neural networks, an architecture that enables parallel token processing and improves sequence modeling capabilities [113]. The Transformer architecture, introduced by [84], is based on the multi-head attention mechanism, which allows the model to assign different weights to words within a context, enhancing its understanding of semantic relationships in text. The training of LLMs consists of multiple stages that involve large-scale data processing and model refinement. In the case of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT), the model undergoes a pre-training phase using diverse textual data, followed by fine-tuning to enhance its performance in conversational interactions [114]. 3.2.8 Natural Language Processing NLP is a subfield of AI that studies methods and techniques to enable computational systems to understand, process, and generate human language [92]. Models based on NLP are widely used in various applications, such as identifying and correcting grammatical errors, disambiguating word meanings, and extracting information [111]. With the advancement of neural network architectures, LLMs have become central to this field, allowing systems to improve in both language understanding and generation [73]. The evolution of LLMs models has introduced challenges related to the limited knowledge embedded within the models and the generation of inaccurate responses [112]. To address these issues, techniques like RAG have been developed, integrating external information retrieval with text generation to enhance response accuracy [48]. This approach enables models to utilize additional information not present in their pre-trained weights, reducing dependence on internally stored data and aligning responses more closely with external sources. The following sections detail the concepts of LLMs, discuss their architecture and functionality, and explain RAG's integration with generative models to improve the quality of generated responses. 3.2.8.1 Large Language Models LLMs can be defined as DL models trained to process and generate natural language based on large volumes of textual data [47] [69]. These models utilize Transformer neural networks, an architecture that enables parallel token processing and improves sequence modeling capabilities [113]. The Transformer architecture, introduced by [84], is based on the multi-head attention mechanism, which allows the model to assign different weights to words within a context, enhancing its understanding of semantic relationships in text. The training of LLMs consists of multiple stages that involve large-scale data processing and model refinement. In the case of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT), the model undergoes a pre-training phase using diverse textual data, followed by fine-tuning to enhance its performance in conversational interactions [114]. This process includes supervised learning, where human trainers provide response examples, and reinforcement learning, in which model-generated responses are ranked to guide further adjustments [115]. Additionally, strategies are implemented to identify and mitigate content deemed

41
inappropriate [116]. The training takes place on large-scale computational infrastructures utilizing thousands of GPUs for data processing and model optimization [117]. Models like GPT use deep neural networks to understand and generate text [118]. With 175 billion parameters, GPT-3.5 Turbo (https://platform.openai.com/docs/model-index-for-researchers), used in this thesis, offers significant improvements over earlier models. GPT-4 (https://openai.com/index/gpt-4), on the other hand, introduced advancements in text comprehension and generation capabilities, with superior performance compared to GPT-3.5. Meanwhile, GPT-4o’s integrated additional functionalities, including multimodality with text, image, and audio input and output support, provide faster responses (https://openai.com/index/hello-gpt-4o ). While LLMs have advanced in various areas, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding studies focused on disseminating information on complex topics, especially in the public administration sector. RAG is a technique that combines information retrieval with text generation to provide more accurate and grounded responses [48]. Unlike fine-tuning, which requires training the model with specific data to improve accuracy, RAG searches external sources to create responses. Despite limitations and challenges, combining LLMs with RAG can be an effective tool for addressing socially relevant issues and improving the dissemination of information on complex topics. Here, we use LLM coupled to RAG to disseminate information, in lay terms, on risks of public works’ development not being carried out as expected. It is worth noting that GPT-3.5 Turbo stood out among other models due to its response time through the OpenAI API, its ability to integrate the use of RAG, and its more affordable cost option. Models like GPT-4 and LLAMA (https://llama.meta.com/), although they may provide advanced capabilities in certain aspects, were considered less viable due to requiring a higher financial investment and not offering the same features for the use of external data via API, which is essential for the interactivity required by the chatbot as part of the solution we propose here for the technical problem at hand.

3.2.8.2 Retrieval-Augmented Generation The RAG technique integrates information retrieval and text generation, allowing LLMs to access external data to support their responses. Unlike traditional models that generate responses solely based on the knowledge stored during training, RAG combines a retrieval mechanism that extracts information from external databases before generating text, making responses more precise and aligned with updated information [48]. RAG can be implemented in different ways, depending on the strategy used for information retrieval. Common approaches include lexical search methods (such as BM25) [119] and vector representation [120], which combine different techniques to enhance the relevance of retrieved documents. The model used in this research employs a vector-based approach to retrieve relevant documents before generating responses, utilizing the LangChain library (https://python.langchain.com/) in combination with GPT-3.5-Turbo. Vector representation enables text to be converted into numerical sequences that can be compared mathematically. This process is carried out through embeddings, which assign each text a vector. In the model used in this research, the OpenAI API generates vectors with 1536 dimensions (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings), each representing a semantic feature of the text. This means that sentences with similar meanings produce vectors that are closer together, whereas sentences with distinct meanings generate more distant vectors. For example, when processing the phrase “risks in public contracts”, the model may generate a vector such as [0.12, -0.34, 0.87, ..., 0.45]. If another phrase, such as “problems in government bidding processes”, is converted into a similar vector, this indicates that the texts share a related meaning. The comparison between these vectors is performed using cosine similarity [121], which measures the angle between two vectors to determine the degree of semantic similarity between texts. This vector representation ensures that information retrieval is based on text meaning rather than exact word matching. Thus, in the implementation of RAG in this research, the process begins with the indexing of documents loaded from a directory. These documents are processed and converted into vector representations using embeddings, which transform text segments into numerical vectors. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. To answer RQ3, the research focused on identifying the key applications, technologies, and challenges reported in the literature regarding the use of Generative AI in the public sector. The objective was to analyze how these solutions have been adapted to meet the specific needs of different governmental contexts, particularly in making complex concepts accessible to diverse stakeholders, including auditors and the general public, who may not have expertise in AI or in the intricacies of public sector operations. Furthermore, as this review included studies published in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, search terms, synonyms, and search strings were adapted for each language.

Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. This procedure ensured data consistency and facilitated subsequent filtering and selection of the most relevant information. Among the sources consulted, Google Scholar stands out for indexing a broad range of publications, including grey literature such as institutional and governmental reports, often unavailable in other digital libraries. However, the platform does not provide a native option for exporting references in CSV format, necessitating manual data collection. Each relevant article had to be individually added to the favorites within the platform for further analysis. Additionally, due to Google Scholar restrictions on automated data extraction via crawlers, automation could not be employed. Given the large number of records returned by Google Scholar, sample refinement was necessary. For this purpose, results were sorted by relevance. As discussed by [126], studies indicate that the most relevant works tend to appear on the initial pages of search results, a phenomenon referred to as “saturation”. Consequently, records from the (𝑛 + 1)ᵗʰ page were considered only when those on the 𝑛ᵗʰ page remained relevant based on a preliminary assessment of their titles.
4.1.7 Removal of Duplicates The exclusion of duplicate studies was conducted in two stages. Initially, a Python script automatically identified potential duplicates based on title similarity and publication year. Subsequently, the abstracts of the studies flagged as duplicates were compared to verify their textual and conceptual equivalence. When a study was confirmed as a duplicate, the less recent version was classified as irrelevant, assigned the exclusion criterion “EC1”, and documented according to the process stage in which it was removed. This procedure ensured the elimination of redundancies, retaining only unique studies for subsequent stages of the analysis. This approach aimed to maintain the integrity of the study selection process, preventing biases arising from duplicate publications and optimizing the representativeness of the dataset used in the review.

Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Downsampling involves reducing the number of instances in the majority class to match the size of the minority class, thereby preventing the model from favoring the majority class disproportionately. This is an integer (ℕ4) that reflects the operational diversity of the contractor. § Years of Existence of the Contractor (Years) (𝑓D): denotes the number of years the company has been operational, calculated by subtracting the year of its establishment from the current year. It is a binary variable ∈{0,1} that reflects the contractor’s compliance status. § Number of Districts Served (𝑓F): measures the number of districts where the contractor has projects and it is defined as 𝑓F = 𝑐𝑜𝑢𝑛𝑡 ({ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑡𝑠 𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑒𝑑 }). The ten above features were adopted from research related to public contract management and risk prediction in projects. The relevance of each is grounded in established theories and concepts from academic literature. For instance, the premise that past performance [129] [130] [131] is indicative of future success in contract bidding scenarios highlights why historical participation and outcomes are critical in assessing a bidder's reliability, as it will be further explained next. Features 𝑓$ and 𝑓%, which illustrate participation profiles, are often associated with the history of companies in procurement processes. As highlighted in [129], performance in public construction tenders can be influenced by phenomena such as the “winner's curse” (where a contractor may win a bid by underestimating costs or overestimating the value of the contract, leading to reduced profitability or potential losses) or the effects of prior experience. Such phenomena suggest that the overall history of participation and outcomes in bidding reflect a contractor's competitiveness and experience, factors that directly impact their performance in future contracts. Feature 𝑓5, which indicates punishment history, was included based on organizational learning theory. This dimension considers that a company's history of project failures may indicate future behavioral patterns. As highlighted in [130], public managers' decisions to sanction contractors are influenced by prior performance issues, making punishment history a significant predictor of potential risks in future contracts. Features 𝑓6 and 𝑓E relate to bidding properties and align with the literature that indicates that factors such as the type of bidding can directly influence risk by affecting competition among bidders, the clarity of established criteria, and the structure of the procurement process. These elements can impact the predictability and efficiency of contract execution [131]. Features 𝑓C and 𝑓D, represent company attributes and align with strategic concepts from business and organizational studies. Research indicates that companies often adopt hybrid strategies, influenced by their operational scope and sector-specific demands, which can affect their resilience and adaptability in competitive markets. Each of these points is described below: i. Clarity of Responses: This criterion evaluated the chatbot's organization, coherence, and language when presenting information about public works and estimated risks. The analysis focused on the structure of the responses and their clarity, ensuring that the information was conveyed objectively, precisely, and comprehensibly while reducing the complexity of the concepts involved. ii. Ease of Use: This criterion examined the intuitiveness of the interaction with the chatbot, considering potential usability challenges. The objective was to determine whether navigating the system was accessible for users with different experience levels, including those unfamiliar with AI-based tools. iii. Accuracy of Responses: This criterion assessed the accuracy of the chatbot's responses by evaluating their consistency with the available system data. title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

experience using it and the reasons behind their assessment. Additionally, participants were provided with a space for further comments, allowing them to express any observations not covered by the other questions. Brazilian users conducted all interactions between the user and the system in Portuguese. Participants were recruited by snowballing through research group announcements, personal contacts, email list invitations, and social media sharing. The system was hosted on a server, and the access link was sent along with the evaluation questionnaire. Before the interaction, participants attended a videoconference where only the system's basic functionalities were presented, such as the listing of public works, the ability to navigate through this list, and the option to view the risk assessments calculated by an AI model. Additionally, it was demonstrated how users could ask the chatbot questions about the information displayed, allowing them to explore details related to the selected project. This procedure aimed to ensure a minimal necessary understanding for its use without influencing user interactions. After this introduction, participants had full autonomy to explore the system. The evaluation questionnaire was completed after usage, allowing responses to reflect each participant’s individual experience. Results for the SLR, risk prediction and communication to lay person are presented in the next Section.

Chapter 4 5. Results and Discussions This section presents the results obtained based on the methodology outlined in the previous chapter. The stages addressed include domain understanding, the development of the risk prediction model, and the processes aimed at knowledge dissemination. Each section to follow details the findings related to each of these stages, discussing the observed implications. 5.1 Domain Understanding This section discusses the collected studies that met the SLR selection criteria to answer RQs 1 to 4. Initially, 3,252 records were identified from the digital libraries. Subsequently, 123 reports were assessed for eligibility, of which 83 were excluded based on various exclusion criteria such as relevance, quality, and completeness. The 40 selected studies exhibit variations across different categories, as detailed in Table 6 (all retrieved studies can be viewed at https://joaquimcmh.github.io/artificial-intelligence-pwcm/?step=0). Regarding the type of publication, the studies primarily consist of conference papers (16), journal articles (15), and dissertations (7), along with a smaller number of magazines (1), and undergraduate capstone projects (1). In terms of language, the majority of studies are published in English (32), while a smaller number are in Portuguese (8). None of the selected studies were published in Spanish, despite the presence of studies originating from Spanish-speaking countries. The data sources used in these studies originate from various countries and regions. Brazil is the primary data source, with 14 studies, followed by Italy (3 studies). Additionally, there are regional groups, such as Greece, Switzerland, Colombia, the USA, Taiwan, and Spain, each contributing 2 studies per region (12 in total). Other countries, including China, Poland, European Union data, Paraguay, Croatia, Russia, the Philippines, Finland, and Turkey, account for 1 study per region (9 in total). Moreover, 2 studies did not specify their data source. Regarding the data type used, most studies relied on open data (20 studies), whereas 15 studies used unpublished data. Furthermore, 4 studies did not provide detailed information about their data sources, and 1 used other public data types. This suggests that, although open data access is predominant, a significant portion of studies still rely on unpublished data or lack transparency in data reporting, which may affect the transparency and reproducibility of the results. abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.

Other frequently employed dimensions include geographic activity, political activity, and participation profile in bids and contracts, which are applied to various targets such as fraud or corruption detection and the prediction of contractual failure risk. These features will be used in constructing predictive models and evaluated in the context of PWCM (please see “Predictive Risk Models” ahead).

Responding to RQ2, the analysis reveals that AI applications in PWCM primarily focus on predictive modeling, leveraging ML-based approaches to estimate various aspects of public contracting processes. The identified targets encompass a broad range of objectives, including cost estimation, fraud detection, execution time prediction, and contractual risk assessment. The diversity of targets demonstrates the versatility of AI in addressing challenges in procurement and contract management. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of feature selection and grouping, as different dimensions play key roles in shaping model performance. While certain dimensions, like bidding and contractual properties, are widely used, others remain underexplored, suggesting opportunities for further research. These findings reinforce the growing role of AI in enhancing decision-making and risk mitigation in public works contracts while also indicating areas where additional studies could refine and expand its applications. 5.1.3 Key Applications, Technologies, and Challenges of Generative AI in Public Procurement The systematic literature review identified six relevant studies exploring the application of generative artificial intelligence in the context of public procurement. These works provide an overview of the key applications, technologies, and challenges associated with the use of LLMs in this domain. The study [61] demonstrated the use of RAG systems combining model Application Program Interfaces (APIs) such as OpenAI and Cohere to optimize the management of legal datasets in public procurement processes. This approach proved effective in suggesting similar documents and tenders, validated through an Italian dataset supervised by experts. However, challenges related to computational costs and occasional API request errors were highlighted, indicating the need for scalable infrastructure and technical improvements. A tool called the Artificial Intelligence Procurement Assistant (AIPA) was proposed in [62] to streamline the evaluation of bids in public procurement processes. Based on LLMs, AIPA was designed to reduce human bias and optimize the relevance and efficiency of results. While practical tests demonstrated positive reception, challenges were noted in ensuring search result relevance and managing large volumes of public procurement data.

The use of generative AI for the analysis and drafting of legal contracts was investigated in [63], where it presented a RAG-based application for summarizing and generating contractual clauses. Despite its theoretical potential, limitations in processing lengthy documents and the lack of extensive empirical testing pointed to the need for advances in user feedback integration and the adoption of more robust models. The studies in [64] and [65] focused on risk detection and the analysis of complex construction contracts. Both studies proposed methods, such as multi-step text segmentation and machine learning models, to improve the efficiency and accuracy of extracting contractual information. These studies highlighted the benefits of automation but also identified limitations, such as the need to balance computational efficiency and performance in models processing long texts. Finally, [66] explored the extraction of award criteria in Swiss tenders using a language model specialized in German. The research addressed challenges such as unstructured data and sustainability criteria, achieving notable precision metrics. However, the computational resource intensity required to operate these systems remains a barrier. The above findings from the SLR offer a base to explore a response to RQ3. While existing studies explore the use of generative AI to address specific tasks in public procurement, such as document retrieval, bid evaluation, and contractual analysis, they largely overlook its application in translating complex insights into accessible knowledge for diverse stakeholders. This gap is particularly critical in public procurement, where effective communication of analytical outputs can bridge the divide between technical experts, policymakers, and lay folk. While RAG systems have shown potential in organizing and contextualizing large datasets, their capacity to facilitate cross-stakeholder understanding remains underexplored. Addressing this limitation could enable the development of generative AI solutions tailored to enhance transparency, foster engagement, and support informed decision-making across varied audiences. These findings suggest that future research should investigate the role of generative AI in structuring and disseminating actionable insights, thereby advancing its applicability in inclusive public procurement processes.

The following outlines the main research gaps identified and future directions that may guide the research agenda in this field. One of the main challenges reported in the reviewed works is the (un)availability of data, a fact also observed in the systematic review where 50% of the data used by the works do not come from open data sources. Although public organizations usually publish data on contracts, these data are often not annotated, meaning they are not classified and labeled to train predictive models. This hinders the proper training of AI-based approaches and makes fraud detection difficult. In addition to the lack of labels, the study [24] also reported difficulty in using textual content in public contracts due to the unstructured content edited by different users, making precise data extraction challenging. Finally, another reported obstacle was the imbalance of classes, commonly observed in events such as frauds, where the proportion of the class under study is small relative to the total sample. This problem can reduce the importance of the smaller class in classification algorithms [35]. The reviewed studies point to experimentation with additional features as a primary theme for future research. 5.1.4 Overall Findings and Key Research Gaps The SLR revealed several challenges and gaps in implementing AI in the context of PWCM. The following outlines the main research gaps identified and future directions that may guide the research agenda in this field. One of the main challenges reported in the reviewed works is the (un)availability of data, a fact also observed in the systematic review where 50% of the data used by the works do not come from open data sources. Although public organizations usually publish data on contracts, these data are often not annotated, meaning they are not classified and labeled to train predictive models. This hinders the proper training of AI-based approaches and makes fraud detection difficult. In addition to the lack of labels, the study [24] also reported difficulty in using textual content in public contracts due to the unstructured content edited by different users, making precise data extraction challenging. Finally, another reported obstacle was the imbalance of classes, commonly observed in events such as frauds, where the proportion of the class under study is small relative to the total sample. This problem can reduce the importance of the smaller class in classification algorithms [35]. The reviewed studies point to experimentation with additional features as a primary theme for future research. New features to be considered in predictions include the number of materials and total project area [31]; weather conditions and efficiency rate [28]; commercial data on the winning bidder (main activity, annual turnover, number of employees, financial situation) [124]; items and their market prices [145]; and geotechnical data of the region [25]. It was also suggested to build models with markers developed by experts [145], recommendations to deepen the influence of each variable both quantitatively [33] and qualitatively [34], comparison of class balancing techniques, and modeling in other specific subareas of contracting [33]. Generative AI applications have demonstrated potential in several areas of public procurement, such as optimizing legal dataset management using RAG systems [61], bid evaluation using LLM-based tools like AIPA [62], and summarizing contractual clauses [63]. However, significant challenges remain. Studies emphasize computational costs, API limitations, and the scalability of infrastructure as barriers to broader adoption. Additionally, issues such as managing large datasets, balancing model efficiency and performance, and limited empirical validation hinder the practical implementation of these solutions. None of the reviewed works specifically address how Generative AI can

79
be leveraged to translate complex insights from public procurement into actionable and accessible knowledge for diverse stakeholders, such as citizens and non-technical managers. This gap highlights the need for focused efforts to bridge technical outputs and stakeholder needs, fostering transparency and engagement. To fill the gaps identified in the state of the art, the following directions for future research are suggested: § Exploration of Class Balancing Techniques: Compare different class balancing techniques to evaluate the improvement in the accuracy of predictive models. Studies can explore techniques such as SMOTE [147], and ADASYN (Adaptive Synthetic Sampling) [147] to enhance the performance of models on imbalanced datasets. Empirical comparisons and studies can provide relevant insights into applying these techniques in various public contracting scenarios – such as risk of contractual failure. § Incorporation of Additional Features: Expand predictive models by including additional features, such as the number of materials, total project area, weather conditions, and commercial data of the winning bidder, which still needs to be widely evaluated in the context of public contracting. Additionally, validating dimensions that have not yet been analyzed for specific objectives, as shown by the gaps in Figure 20, is a promising direction for future research. § Qualitative and Quantitative Evaluation of Features: Explore the influence of qualitative and quantitative features to enhance the understanding of factors impacting contracting outcomes. Studies can focus on sensitivity analysis to determine which features have the most significant impact on predictions and how these features interact with each other. § Long-Term Model Evaluation: Study the relevance and effectiveness of predictive models in real production contexts over time. Consider variations in dependent and independent variables (features), which can degrade the predictive power of the models. Research can explore techniques for continuous monitoring and model updating to maintain their accuracy and relevance over time. § Definition of Success Indicators: Identify and define specific success indicators for applying AI in public contracting, including metrics such as resource savings, reduction in decision-making and supervision time or costs, increased transparency, and reduced fraud and corruption. Future studies can develop frameworks for the quantitative and qualitative evaluation of these indicators, providing a precise measure of the impact of AI in public contracting.

§ Knowledge Dissemination: Explore Generative AI methodologies, such as fine-tuned language models and RAG systems, to create accessible and actionable insights from complex procurement data. This includes evaluating methods to adapt these tools to stakeholder-specific requirements and addressing computational cost challenges. The lack of such solutions in current studies indicates a promising direction for linking technical outputs to practical, stakeholder-driven goals. 5.1.5 Limitations and Threats to Validity A limitation of the SLR conducted arises from the impossibility of precisely comparing the models reported in the selected articles. This difficulty stems from the heterogeneity of measurement units and evaluation metrics employed by the studies, such as distinct currencies and varying methodological approaches used to assess the performance of ML models. Another limiting factor is that the review did not exclusively consider studies specifically focused on the public works sector. Some selected articles have a broader scope, encompassing the overall public procurement process, including not only public works but also procurement of goods and various types of services by government entities. Additionally, potentially relevant works identified in the references of the articles included in this review were unavailable for full consultation at the time of analysis. Therefore, future research could utilize the snowballing technique to expand the literature coverage, enabling a more comprehensive and in-depth analysis of studies published in this area. Finally, another limitation is that the reviewed studies were not categorized according to different stakeholders involved in the public procurement process, such as oversight institutions, entities conducting the bidding processes, and the general population benefiting from public works. Such categorization could facilitate a clearer understanding of the impact, interests, and specific requirements of these various groups regarding the use of ML models within the context of public procurement.

5.2 Predictive Risk Models This section answers RQ5. For that we conducted some experiments with the AI algorithms RF, ANN, LR and SGB. Table 9 presents a comparison of ML models’ performances using different data balancing methods, evaluated by the ROC-AUC metric.
In the initial comparative experiment, using the original dataset, the training data for the classification models were imbalanced, with 37% of the contracts being classified as having undergone the contract termination process. Based on the results, the LR model achieved the highest ROC-AUC score of 0.66, indicating a moderate ability to differentiate between high-risk and low-risk contracts. The RF and SGB models both showed a ROC-AUC of 0.5, suggesting these models could not effectively distinguish between the classes. The ANN performed slightly better with a ROC-AUC of 0.54. The insufficient dataset likely led to inadequate model training, causing a classification bias towards the majority class (low risk) as a strategy to minimize error rates in the face of sparse high-risk examples. After applying the undersampling technique to balance the classes in the training set, the resulting sample contained 192 records, with 96 for each class. The RF model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.64, showing some improvement. The SGB model also showed a slight improvement with a ROC-AUC of 0.62. The ANN model had a ROC-AUC of 0.61, indicating a fair performance. However, the LR model's performance decreased significantly with a ROC-AUC of 0.5, suggesting that undersampling may not be an effective balancing technique for this model.

with the original sample (95% CI: [0.46, 0.81]). The undersampling technique and the RF model had the lowest ROC-AUC of 0.64 (95% CI: [0.57, 0.72]). The confusion matrices in Figure 21 provide a detailed view of the classifiers' performance. Each matrix shows the number of true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN). In the case of LR with original data, the model correctly identified 8 failure contracts (TP) and 98 normal contracts (TN), but incorrectly classified 20 normal contracts as failures (FP) and 34 failure contracts as normal (FN). The results show that machine learning-based classifiers can effectively identify risks, as evidenced by ROC-AUC values exceeding the threshold of 0.5 (random classifier). The RF model with oversampling achieved the best performance among the evaluated approaches, with an AUC of 0.75 and a confidence interval ranging from 0.64 to 0.87. LG using the original sample reached an AUC of 0.66, with a wider confidence interval ([0.46, 0.81]), indicating greater uncertainty. The RF with undersampling showed a lower AUC of 0.64, with a narrower interval ([0.57, 0.72]), but inferior performance. These results suggest that, although performance varies across models and balancing strategies, the combination of oversampling and RF yielded the most favorable outcomes for risk prediction. It remains to investigate the importance that input features have on the predicted risk levels. The variable importance values were calculated using the RF model with oversampling, demonstrating the best performance among the evaluated models. The variable importance analysis was conducted using the Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI) method [148], which measures the average reduction in impurity each variable provides when splitting the data at decision nodes in the forest.

The importance analysis revealed that project value (𝑓G) and size (𝑓$4) are relevant factors in risk prediction, with the importance of 0.1676 and 0.1401, respectively. These findings are consistent with other studies indicating that projects with larger capital investments involve more stakeholders, have more activities and goals, and increase administrative complexity [53]. Additionally, the company's operating time (𝑓D), the number of districts served (𝑓F), and the number of pending information items (𝑓E) were also significant, with the importance of 0.1482, 0.1286, and 0.1134, respectively. The company's operating time can be seen as an indicator of experience, whereas companies that have been in operation for longer periods generally have more mature processes and a greater capacity to manage risks. The estimated duration directly affects resource allocation, schedules, and costs, and long-term projects are more exposed to changes in external conditions. The number of pending information items may indicate problems in communication and document management, increasing the probability of errors and failures or even the omission of information by the contracted company. The total number of bids won (𝑓$) did not significantly influence risk prediction, which may indicate that simply winning bids is not a determining factor in the project's risk assessment. On the other hand, the total number of bids contested (𝑓%), with an importance of 0.1129, may indicate the company's ability to actively compete for contracts, suggesting familiarity with the bidding process and a potential ability to identify and mitigate risks. However, many contested bids may also point to difficulties in winning these bids, revealing possible weaknesses in proposals or challenges in fully meeting the required specifications. Finally, the number of activities (𝑓C), with an importance of 0.0997, reflects the company's operational diversity. Companies with a higher number of activities may face additional challenges in coordinating and managing resources, which can increase the risks of project failures due to internal operational complexities 5.2.2 Limitations and Threats to Validity A limitation of the risk modeling study is that the data used for risk prediction (and also knowledge dissemination) came exclusively from governments in Brazil. While this allows for a detailed and contextualized analysis of the country's specificities, it is recommended that other studies include data from other countries to verify the applicability and robustness of the models developed in different international contexts.

Additionally, the study was constrained by data availability, as only datasets from the state of Paraíba in Brazil were ultimately used due to challenges in obtaining and processing data from other states. Data from Pernambuco, São Paulo, and Rio Grande do Sul were evaluated; however, limitations such as incomplete contract records, lack of structured information on public works, and difficulties in integrating datasets prevented their inclusion in the final model (see https://joaquimcmh.github.io/artificial-intelligence-pwcm/?step=1). Future work should explore different resampling methods to assess their impact on model effectiveness. 5.3 Knowledge Dissemination To answer research questions RQ6 and RQ7, the developed system for information on public works and their risks, including its LLM-RAG chatbot, was presented to 35 evaluators. The full system link was provided to each participant, allowing them to use the application freely, with the authors direct monitoring their interactions. Regarding demographic data, the average age of the participating evaluators was 38 years, with an age range from 19 to 54 years. Regarding gender distribution, there were 19 males, 14 females, and two individuals identified as other. In terms of education, 16 participants reported having completed high school, 14 had a university degree, and 5 had a postgraduate degree. Questions were also included to assess the participants' understanding of AI. The results indicated that 20 participants did not know the subject, 10 had a basic understanding, 4 had moderate knowledge, and only one demonstrated advanced knowledge. In parallel with their knowledge of AI, the participants' familiarity with public works was also evaluated. Most categorized their knowledge of public works as basic (18), 16 indicated no knowledge, and only one claimed advanced knowledge.

This limitation may affect the generalization of the findings, as regional variations in public works contracts, procurement practices, and risk factors may influence model performance. Another limitation is related to the data balancing techniques used in the predictive modeling process. The study employed oversampling and undersampling to handle class imbalance; however, more advanced techniques, such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), were not utilized. The lack of SMOTE may have impacted the classifier’s ability to generate synthetic examples for the minority class, potentially limiting improvements in predictive performance. Future work should explore different resampling methods to assess their impact on model effectiveness. 5.3 Knowledge Dissemination To answer research questions RQ6 and RQ7, the developed system for information on public works and their risks, including its LLM-RAG chatbot, was presented to 35 evaluators. The full system link was provided to each participant, allowing them to use the application freely, with the authors direct monitoring their interactions. Regarding demographic data, the average age of the participating evaluators was 38 years, with an age range from 19 to 54 years. Regarding gender distribution, there were 19 males, 14 females, and two individuals identified as other. In terms of education, 16 participants reported having completed high school, 14 had a university degree, and 5 had a postgraduate degree. Questions were also included to assess the participants' understanding of AI. The results indicated that 20 participants did not know the subject, 10 had a basic understanding, 4 had moderate knowledge, and only one demonstrated advanced knowledge. In parallel with their knowledge of AI, the participants' familiarity with public works was also evaluated. Most categorized their knowledge of public works as basic (18), 16 indicated no knowledge, and only one claimed advanced knowledge.

title: Inteligência artificial na gestão de contratos de obras públicas: previsão de riscos e disseminação de conhecimento para o público leigo.
abstract: A Administração Pública contrata aproximadamente USD 13 trilhões anualmente, com 20% desse valor destinado a obras públicas, como a construção de infraestruturas. Apesar das leis e regras, não é incomum que obras públicas enfrentem atrasos ou até mesmo sejam abandonadas antes de sua conclusão. Esses problemas não apenas resultam em desperdício de recursos públicos, mas também prejudicam o desenvolvimento econômico e social das regiões afetadas. Embora os cidadãos possam contribuir para a gestão de contratos de obras públicas (PWCM, na sigla em inglês) – e.g., monitorando o progresso das obras e sinalizando possíveis problemas –, eles podem não compreender os conceitos complexos necessários para uma participação efetiva. Essa falta de compreensão pode resultar em oportunidades perdidas para intervenções e fiscalizações oportunas por parte da sociedade. Esta tese investiga como a Inteligência Artificial (AI, na sigla em inglês) pode apoiar a PWCM. Especificamente, explora como a AI pode modelar riscos, simplificar conceitos complexos de projetos e comunicá-los para o público leigo. Para isso, o estudo emprega uma abordagem abrangente, envolvendo entendimento do domínio, predição de riscos e disseminação de conhecimentos. A fase de entendimento do domínio envolveu uma Revisão Sistemática da Literatura (SLR, na sigla em inglês), analisando 3.252 estudos publicados entre 2010 e 2024. Essa revisão mapeou aplicações atuais de AI, destacou lacunas nas fases dos contratos públicos, nos objetivos dessas aplicações, nos algoritmos empregados, nas características utilizadas na construção de modelos de aprendizado de máquina (ML, na sigla em inglês) e ofereceu uma visão abrangente sobre técnicas preditivas e de IA generativa no setor de obras públicas. Com base em uma parcela dos achados da SLR, quatro modelos de ML foram desenvolvidos e avaliados para prever o risco de falha contratual de obras, utilizando dados da Paraíba, Brasil. Entre eles, o modelo Random Forest, fazendo uso de oversampling para balanceamento de dados, obteve desempenho superior, com um valor de ROC-AUC de 0,75. Para auxiliar os usuários leigos, foi desenvolvido um sistema integrado a uma interface de chatbot, que exibe informações sobre obras públicas e seus respectivos riscos. O sistema foi desenvolvido utilizando um modelo de linguagem de grande escala (LLM, na sigla em inglês), com o objetivo de responder às dúvidas dos usuários de forma simplificada e facilitar a compreensão de riscos e detalhes dos projetos. Testado com 35 participantes de diferentes níveis de conhecimento sobre PWCM, o chatbot obteve aprovação significativa em termos de clareza, utilidade prática, precisão, facilidade de uso e confiabilidade, promovendo a compreensão dos processos de PWCM. Este estudo avança o conhecimento sobre aplicações de IA na PWCM e oferece diretrizes para a integração de tais ferramentas em sistemas governamentais, promovendo uma participação cidadã mais informada nos assuntos públicos.
